before: Regarding some corruption. Prov 12, 14. He brings in the corrupted one, reproaching himself as one who hated instruction, and says: 'I would have perished even if I had not been corrupted, having wasted my flesh in dissipation, and having made this life small.' Therefore it became evident that my discipline was in the midst of the Church and the Synagogue. For the voice has repented, and not having occurred, it has become little by little. Similar is the saying, 'By little by little my waters were poured out' (Song 8:16). For having recovered and having perceived, he says: 'Where is the little by little?' How then can one console the madness which is from nature?

Prov 15. Knowledge is both a cistern and a fountain; to those coming to the virtues it is a cistern, but to those perfected by them, a fountain. And knowledge is called mother, and wife, and sister; mother, because through her we are born by the teacher; wife, because being joined it brings forth virtues and right doctrines; sister, because from one God we have become. And I called wisdom sister.
Prov 19, 17. See how it shows not only ease through abundance, but also having no one a partner in enjoyment; and it doubles itself and calls it possession; for one knows the pleasure of the matter.

Prov 6. Even if you imitate the natural work of the irrational: or be, that is, go forth. For many do good works from theory or hearing, and not from knowledge. A prophet and apostles say [it is like] bees, whose labors are useful to the great for their order and to the small; he says the matters are the wax, but the honey is the contemplation of these things. Just as the shepherd guides the goats, so the essence guides the bees. Therefore, in all things, order is good for life.
Prov 12. The fool is the atheist who has lost the theoretical, but the lawless one is he who has lost the practical.

Signifying many things, as we have said, the principle now denotes the eternal, and the cause, and the productive. And the principle of some things is a principle, and signifies a relation, but not subsistence. For things toward something are such: as the right and the left. Therefore, the Wisdom of God, being a subsistence, is not a principle of any things; for before creation, Wisdom exists. But when it receives a relation toward created things, then it becomes a principle of the productive and providential ways of God, toward the works which have their existence from the Creator, having contributed nothing to it toward being Wisdom; but the relation through which it is called principle and creator, that came to be when the created things came to be. For a principle does not pre-exist those of which it is a principle; nor are these said to exist with it, if the creatures possess their subsistence in time. For Wisdom, being eternal, is not subject to time.

3 Therefore the principle is a spouse to the creatures. The Son of God, pre-existing the creation, being Wisdom, if he says, 'The Lord created me,' he does not have the thought of subsistence, but rather a relation toward the creatures. For he says he is created for works, being the principle of the productive and providential ways of God, that is to say, the cause, to speak more introductory. The Son of God has become man, taking the form of a slave; and being from before the ages and eternal, in that which God is the Word, he is said to be created because he had birth from Mary, becoming flesh; so that those who wish to walk according to God and toward God may use a teacher, providing a pattern of excellent life and instruction to those who follow.

That 'created' does not always signify subsistence, is shown by David saying, 'Create in me a clean heart, O God' (Psalm 51:10). For he asks not as one not possessing, to receive, but as one having cast it away, to receive it again having been cleansed. And Paul, saying the two are created into one new man (Ephesians 2:15), does not signify the subsistence of men, but a union from concord; just as those who interpreted 'He created me' brought it forth. before: A proverb is such as, 'Sweet is war to the inexperienced,' and, 'A woman penetrating hollows bores through rock.' The proverb is said [to be such]: for in the beginning, when the things now called 'milestones' by the Romans were still insignificant, then called 'signs,' the ancients used to set up places along a certain road, and upon these they wrote certain matters. For they did this for two reasons: to make known to the traveler the distance of the road, and for the one reading the inscription, becoming acquainted with its clarity, to be relieved of his fatigue. For a milestone is called the road.

. To know words of prudence is, principally, to make virtue manifest, just as the other interpreters clarify, having handed down [them] as words not of prudence, but of understanding. Either he says 'words of prudence' regarding those which are sophistical and cunning.
. The word rebuking those who are imitating righteousness, and saying they have it as is necessary, says: 'If then you truly speak righteousness, judge uprightly, you sons of men' (Prov 2:9).

. I hear the interpretation of Theodotus, which Symmachus also handed down, that they have presented a problem. What then is the obscure saying? That which is poured together according to logos and intellect and phrase; such as that with the prophet Isaiah: 'Woe to the land of ships, beyond the rivers of Ethiopia! He who sends a ship by sea, and letter-books upon the water' (Isa 19:2). For none of these has the word clear either in parables, or a manifest narration of history. And of the enigma, it is to understand the spoken thing, but of the obscure saying, not even the spoken thing. An obscure saying is generally a sound; but a parable is particular; and obscure is not according to a deprivation of light, but the hidden one, as to be darkened for the one who is ignorant. And beautiful sayings are aphorisms; but an enigma is a word with [an] interpretation.
The signs lift up the truth: such is the [meaning of], 'Open, O Lebanon, your gates, and let fire devour your cedars' (Song of Solomon 8:1).

Verse 6. For fear, that is piety according to reverence, is true; and understanding is good. This must be substantiated. For it is not sufficient for blessedness to know the good, unless one also does it; and piety toward God is the beginning of understanding.

Verse 7. God is the Father of the righteous. For everyone who does righteousness is from God. And our Mother is the Church, whose bridegroom is our Lord Jesus Christ. And the laws are the apostolic ordinances.

Even if the preceding [words] have an upward leading, they are also applied to parents according to nature, when they, being God-fearing, rear the children. And since there is a man, the teacher, who has fathered through the Gospel those being instructed, the Church is spouse to this [man] and mother of those born, or rather, the ecclesiastical opinion and way of life.

Therefore, says the proverbs-maker, if you, to me, now as a teacher and father, but now as wisdom and virtue instead of a mother you listen to, you shall be crowned with a crown of grace, and your neck shall be adorned with a golden collar, fashioned from intellectual gold and gems. For the head of the inner man, the domain of virtues, is revealed to be the material of a crown, which are called graces. In agreement with the crown, being intellectual, the golden collar placed upon the neck of the soul—that is, its submissive part—must also be included.

Verse 8. And regarding the head and neck, he speaks of the mind; and the golden collar, of knowledge and the intellectual adornment of the soul; or the golden collar, of the submission to God and the domain of the divine sayings.
Verse 9. And being with others indeed leads to sinning, it brings punishments; men indeed are impious, those perfect in wickedness.

Verse 10. Those whom they might persuade to think of earthly things, they hide in the earth; but a righteous man you will perceive to have a heavenly mindset. These things can also be understood in reference to Christ, and in reference to the...

before: He stood by him, and he is before all things. And the Lord himself says: 'I am the beginning of the creation of God' (Revelation 3:14). For just as a man undergoes becoming, desiring to be a foundation of the Church so that it might be established upon him without being shaken, so also, desiring to provide being to the creation, it has happened according to that, introducing the aforementioned relationship, becoming a beginning and a cause to those who are to come; but even if, he says, it was created according to these things, yet before all things God begets me, which is the Son.

He says that He takes the throne as his own kingdom, and the spiritual forces as winds; or just as David: 'He who walks on the wings of the winds' (Ps 135:6); desiring to present the less tangible part of his being as immaterial.
See the works being divided: wisdom and God. One was making, he says; but I was joining. And strong, how? We need no foundation, for it is upheld by the will of God alone.

Either that at the same time as appearing he provides life, or that he comes forth to reveal to someone descending toward the weakness of the mind there; for being life, and having come out to those able to see him, he gives life; and he says either will or love, or that he made us autonomous so as to be ready to do what is necessary.
Let him withdraw, that he may gain wisdom; for the imperfect is strengthened by the words and mysteries of wisdom.

The same food and meat are named both bread and milk and wine. Moreover, the foolish are said to partake of their own bread and of poured-out wine; if it is this, how shall we understand? 'A man ate the bread of angels' (Ps 78:25), [meaning] understand for me the solid commands of God as bread, and wine as the knowledge of him from the study of the divine Scriptures; likewise also his divine body and precious blood.

The natural thinker hears, 'The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night' (Ps 121:6). He calls the worldly cares a burning; and those being dried up by it he calls hay; but the Savior, through the parable, indicates the tribulations; and he called the persecutions according to the word a burning.

The ungodly have only evil hopes; for everything they hope for is destruction (Proverbs 10:28).

Verse 7. The phrase, “Instead of him,” does not mean as the subject of the pious man is [subjected] to judgment, but because the snare stands from the evil against the righteous; the pious one is rescued from it by God, but the ungodly, having been abandoned by divine providence, falls into it. Or, because the righteous man is subject to certain things as a man is to sins, but the ungodly having come and having done evil to the righteous, has rescued him from sins and from future punishments, while he himself received the punishments; and he is handed over not by anyone else, but by his own wickedness, as having previously handed himself over to an unproven mind.
Verse 4. Those who gather [things] are diminished from virtues; or, those gathering words and not transmitting them.
Verse 10. He who is harsh regarding each of the defects of his own house will be homeless; but a fool will serve a wise man.

Verse 13. An ungodly man, therefore, he says, is one who hates God; but a sinner is one who is evil regarding his actions; and a righteous man here he calls the practical man with word and knowledge; for the precision of righteousness is great.
Verse 6. “The better” is not comparative, but “instead of the good.”
Verse 9. The practical and the private man is more honorable than the one in word and elegant but inactive.
Verse 12. The roots of the righteous will not be uprooted, that is, the good dispositions.

Verse 7. Whatever he says, he says, is confirmed by works; and if it is more certain by work. Or, instead of [saying] “manifestly,” [it is] “established,” “unimpeachable,” to show it sufficiently himself. But a witness of the unrighteous is one who recommends and attempts what he would unrighteously do; and a deceitful man is one who has nothing upright.

Verse 10. The one speaking of punishments disturbs the one currently walking in a practical life; but the one speaking of promises rejoices. For the perfect righteous man will not be afraid from hearing evil, having fear of the Lord who exalts all (Proverbs 10:16).

Verse 16. The righteous, knowing human weakness, forgives, even if the offense is from a friend; or, because recognizing that the friend is according to the image of God, he is in agreement with himself, being moderate, and guarding himself, and having nothing of the enemy's malice, he holds his thoughts stable.
Verse 2. For the one will have the end of virtue, but the others will not have the fruit.

[St. 14] If a tree of life is nourished from fruits of righteousness, everyone hiding righteousness with injustice, which is called a hand, will not eat from the tree of life. [St. 23] Of your disciples, so that you do not lead the teaching toward outward appearance. [St. 22] He says that the contemplation of events, and the contemplation of the Holy Trinity, is a garment for a pure mind, of fine linen and purple (Proverbs 31:22).

before: The veins of the body are not ruptured before the shedding of blood kills the man; for it drinks blood, and from this it is nourished and grows. In this way he now resembles the parasite. He is the one who is unable to rule by the force of men; for he has made use of three main impulses against them: pleasure, seduction, and deception, and because of this, having undermined them little by little, he overthrows them. First, indeed, he leads them into the paths of false doctrine toward destruction, which is indeed called 'sweetness,' showing the magnitude of sin at its end; then, surrounding them with the pleasure of lawlessness, which is indeed called the lust for women. Upon these is added love of money, that is, greed, which he said cannot even fill the earth with water; for such is the sandy, insatiable thing. These, then, are the passions which the evil one has discovered for the destruction of men, whom he loves and cherishes as if they were his own daughters.

The fourth method he calls the friction and habit of these; for not even one who has falsely believed, or committed fornication, or desired more, immediately fell into these passions, but having been defeated in the remainder by habit and sensation; for such people you would find buried in false doctrines, never receiving a child, but always promoting the passions, as well as inciting others to these things. Just as indeed neither water nor fire ceases at the supply of what is being poured out, nor does it say, 'It is enough,' but rather it becomes an overflowing; the water, by the pouring in of water, does not stop, but increases; which also you, he says, O child, knowing, should abstain from, so that you may not be lost in a short time, like the finest thief, plundering life through pleasure.

The tracks of a soaring eagle are the soul of the wise, which, being wise, is unable to know from itself the flights of the intellectual eagle; about which it is written: 'The great eagle and he who has long wings and is full of claws' (Job 39:26), not having a trace of the presence of the devil, although I did not know from where he flew before me; for the evil one departing from me, I did not know, because I did not have desire toward him. Such is the path of the harlot, the corrupted teaching.

The people from the Gentiles, being formerly a slave to sin and to the devil; thus: 'I greatly vex you with my fury' (Gal 5:20); and, 'O foolish one, filled with the foods of life' (Prov 9:2); and, 'Harlot woman,' which is a prostitute; for the Church from the Gentiles was a prostitute, walking after foreign gods; and a maidservant who casts out her own mistress, the Church of the Gentiles being the Synagogue as mistress; for of this, the law and the prophets are required. The literal investigation is a slave to the intellectual contemplation, which the Jews preferred as a mistress; but the Gentiles, receiving the literal as the spiritual, cast off the physical observance of the law as a mistress among them. He says the Gentiles, who have no strength, and treasure for themselves eternal life through good works. And the pig-rollers; a kind of fish, that is, the so-called hares, the oysters, the former...
